newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Old Yeltsin foe makes comeback, rejects conflict.
newsitem.headline: Old Yeltsin foe makes comeback, rejects conflict.

text.p: Alexander Rutskoi, the former Russian vice-president who became a bitter enemy of Boris Yeltsin completed a remarkable comeback on Monday by being elected governor of the central Kursk region by a landslide.

The victory of Rutskoi, who lost a bloody power struggle with President Yeltsin in 1993, was one of several setbacks for the Kremlin as results came in from a series of regional elections held on Sunday.
However the moustachioed Rutskoi, who won 79 percent of the votes against just 18 percent for Yeltsin-backed incumbent Vasily Shuteyev, quickly struck a conciliatory note.
"We do not intend to wage war with the Kremlin or with the authorities," he told Russian Public Television.

"I have said many times that today's Rutskoi is a different Rutskoi. Now I am not interested in the development of the political situation. I am interested in the development of the economy. The economy determines politics," he said.
His new post will give Rutskoi, 49, a place in the Federation Council, the upper chamber of parliament.

Rutskoi was Yeltsin's running-mate when the Russian president was first elected in 1991. But they soon fell out personally and politically and he was jailed for siding with hardline members of parliament against the president.
He was later pardoned and went back into politics, forming a nationalist movement allied with the opposition communists.
Sunday's polls were part of a series of elections which are gradually being held to elect the regional leaders who make up the Federation Council.
The Kremlin administration is watching the elections closely in the hope that its preferred candidates, mostly current governors nominated by Yeltsin, will consolidate their position.
But they face stiff opposition from contenders representing the National Patriotic Bloc led by the communists.

The communists hope to cash in on the hardships suffered under economic reforms to increase their representation in the Federation Council, where nearly half the 178 members still owe their jobs to Yeltsin.

The opposition already dominates the State Duma (lower house). Winning control of the Federation Council would increase the opposition's ability to block government legislation and overturn presidential decrees or vetoes.

Rutskoi was initially banned from standing by the local electoral commission which said he was ineligible because he had moved out of Kursk, his home region, long ago. But a court reinstated him just two days before the poll.
Rutskoi's comeback is certain to infuriate the Kremlin.
"It's a serious defeat for democracy," said Sergei Belyayev, head of the pro-government Our Home is Russia Duma faction.
Yeltsin chose the Afghan war hero as his running mate in 1991 to woo the votes of reformist communists and the military.
But Rutskoi later took parliament's side when the legal uncertainties following the collapse of communism led to a struggle between the reformist president and the more conservative legislature.
When Yeltsin, putting the constitution aside, tried to dissolve parliament in September 1993, deputies refused to obey and proclaimed Rutskoi their president.

Rutskoi led a bloody uprising in Moscow on October 3. A handful of troops backed by government tanks shelling the parliament ended the protest. Rutskoi and his allies were jailed and the post of vice-president was scrapped.
The new parliament pardoned Rutskoi the following year. He went on to form the nationalist Derzhava movement which backed the communist candidate in this year's presidential election.
In other setbacks in Sunday's polls, an opposition member of parliament became governor in Kirov, a region east of Moscow.

Yeltsin's appointee was defeated in the western enclave of Kaliningrad, and the Pskov region will require a second round of voting. In one success for the Kremlin, the Yeltsin-backed candidate was elected on the far eastern island of Sakhalin.
Before Sunday, the score between the communists and the Kremlin in the regional elections was level.
